sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Historically, stereotactic mesencephalotomy was developed as a “supraspinal” cordotomy for cancer and neuropathic pain. Early experiences relieved pain, but the procedure was never widely adopted because of the associated morbidity with midbrain lesioning. Contemporary image-guided lesioning could make this a feasible procedure for cancer patients suffering with pain.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A single-center, nonrandomized, early phase trial was designed to treat patients with severe, refractory pain from head and neck cancer with unilateral MRI-guided focused ultrasound mesencephalotomy. Safety was the primary outcome, but measures of efficacy were assessed with pain intensity and more functional components of pain.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A discrete midbrain lesion was created for the 5 patients. All patients with advanced cancer had limited survival of less than 3 months, but they tolerated the procedure and experienced pain relief to different degrees. Two had profound pain relief, one was partial, and two others were very brief. One patient was transiently obtunded and other procedural morbidities were mild: numbness (3), oculomotor disturbance (1), and agitation (1). Electroencephalography, somatosensory evoked potentials, and quantitative sensory testing were obtained when possible.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Stereotactic focused ultrasound mesencephalotomy is a modern, image-guided, lesioning technique that may be effective for cancer pain.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Stereotactic mesencephalotomy was a historical procedure developed for cranio-cervical pain related to cancer. While spinal cordotomy proved successful for many cancer pains of the body [1], the need to treat more cephalad pain resulted in more “cranial” spinothalamic lesioning at the levels of the medulla [2], pons [3], and then at the midbrain because of easier access to the nociceptive fibers from a craniotomy [4]. This first mesencephalotomy was performed by Earl Walker in 1942 – sectioning the spinothalamic and secondary trigeminal tracts from a subtemporal approach with “a 5 mm in depth incision from lateral sulcus across the brachium of the inferior colliculus” [4]. The procedure was later performed with stereotactic techniques [5] and then refined with electrical stimulation mapping [6–10]. A review of these early and subsequent trials through the late 1980s reported short-term pain relief for 85% of 272 cases [11]. But stereotactic mesencephalotomy never gained widespread adoption because the procedure lacked the precision to minimize morbidity.

The dorsal midbrain is conceptually appealing as a target for pain intervention as it represents an anatomical confluence of the ascending and descending pain pathways. Additionally, the spinothalamic and spinoreticular tracts include fibers from both the body and the head. Contemporary lesioning with high-intensity focused ultrasound (FUS) coupled with continuous intraoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) thermal monitoring is precise and importantly avoids brain distortion that accompanies cranial opening. This single-center, observational pilot study investigates stereotactic FUS mesencephalotomy for the management of refractory pain associated with head and neck cancer.

sec.title: Study Design
sec.p: This early phase trial was a prospective, unblinded, clinical assessment of stereotactic FUS mesencephalotomy in subjects with treatment-refractory pain from head and neck cancer. Since a midbrain ablation is a novel target for FUS, the study was designed to assess precision of lesioning, safety, tolerability and estimate the degree of pain relief. This trial was also intended to provide insight into midbrain targeting, namely, whether pain relief occurs with medial lesioning of the periaqueductal gray and spinoreticular tract or lateral targeting of the spinothalamic and trigeminothalamic tracts. Neurophysiological measurements were included to evaluate pathophysiology. The trial was IRB approved and registered as NCT03894553.

sec.title: Study Cohort
sec.p: Patients were included if they were between 18 and 85 years of age and presented with severe, refractory, craniocervical pain from head or neck cancer for a duration of more than 3 months. Severe pain was defined when the worst pain over 24 h was ≥5/10 using the numerical pain rating scale (NPRS). Treatment refractory was defined as when all three tiers of the WHO cancer pain classification were trialed and failed. Subjects were included if they suffered from cancer, typically squamous cell carcinoma, localized to the head and neck region. All participants provided informed written consent.

Patients were not eligible for the study if the skull density ratio was less than 0.4. Other craniofacial pain conditions were excluded including trigeminal neuralgia, headache, migraine, temporomandibular joint syndrome, and atypical facial pain. Limited life expectancy of less than 3 months was supposedly ruled out by their oncologist. Patients were included if they were participating in other clinical trials for cancer management, but they were excluded if the treatment was intended for pain relief.

sec.title: FUS Mesencephalotomy
sec.p: On the day of the procedure, patients presented to the FUS suite. An intravenous line was placed and the hair was clipped and shaved. A stereotactic frame was placed with a local anesthetic. The patient was then positioned in the 3T MRI-guided FUS system (Insightec ExAblate Neuro) with a rubber membrane affixed to the scalp. The ultrasound transducer was filled with chilled and degassed water. An anesthesiologist maintained normotension and administered sedation as needed.

Reference imaging was obtained with a volumetric steady-state gradient echo (FIESTA) sequence, and the images were reconstructed in planes orthogonal to the anterior and posterior commissures. Preoperative CT and high-resolution fast gray matter acquisition T1 inversion recovery were fused to the reference images. The midbrain target was selected contralateral to the pain, below the level of the superior colliculus, and either medial at the border of the periaqueductal gray and reticular activating region or more lateral for the spinothalamic and trigeminothalamic tracts. No pass regions for the acoustic beams were designated to the frontal air sinus, intracranial calcifications, and folds in the rubber membrane. Movement detection algorithms were performed during the procedure. A series of alignment sonications were performed to ensure that the natural focus of the transducer matched the two-dimensional plane of the MRI thermal images. Then the therapeutic sonications were performed by escalating the acoustic energy and continuously monitoring the treatment with MR thermometry and clinical assessment. Final ablative temperatures neared 60°C by peak voxel thermometry. The patients were then hospitalized overnight for observation.

sec.title: Clinical Outcomes
sec.p: The primary outcome measure was safety with adverse events collected throughout the study. Safety assessments also include MRI and neuro-ophthalmology evaluation. The pre-specified, primary efficacy assessment was a traditional NPRS measured as the worst pain over 24 h on an 11-point scale. This pain intensity was compared from baseline to 90 days post-procedure. Patients with a ≥50% reduction in NPRS scores were classified as “responders.”

sec.title: MRI Lesion Analysis
sec.p: MRI was obtained for all subjects at baseline and on the day following the procedure (Fig. 1). The following sequences were obtained on a 3 Tesla Siemens Prisma Fit scanner: MPRAGE, volumetric T2 and axial two-dimensional T2, diffusion-weighted, susceptibility-weighted, fast gray matter acquisition T1 inversion recovery, and resting-state functional blood oxygen level-dependent sequences. Manual volumetric segmentation of the ablation region of interest was performed on both T1- and T2-weighted images with 1 millimeter resolution using the free-hand tool on our institution’s Picture Archiving and Communication System. Transcranial FUS lesions have previously been described to have three concentric zones [12]. Lesion volumes (zones 1 and 2) were measured using T1- and T2-weighted sequences on postoperative day 1 images. Additionally, the T2-weighted perilesional edema was segmented to measure zone 3. Lesion coordinates were measured at the center of the lesion and reported in relation to the mid-commissural point.

caption.p: Stereotactic FUS mesencephalotomy. a Axial illustration of the dorsal midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus. Note medial targeting at the junction of the PAG/RAS for spinoreticular or lateral targeting of the spinothalamic or trigeminothalamic tract. b–f Postoperative day 1 MRI of subjects 002, 005, 006, 009, and 010 treated in this series.

sec.title: Resting-State EEG
sec.p: Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) power spectral density (PSD) analysis was performed before and within 1 month after FUS mesencephalotomy. EEG data were acquired at a sampling rate of 1,000 Hz using a BrainAmp MR Plus system (Brain Products GmbH, Gilching, Germany) with electrodes placed according to the international 10–20 system. Electrode impedances were maintained below 10 kilo ohms. During recordings, participants were instructed to remain relaxed with their eyes open, breathing and blinking naturally while minimizing movement. Six minutes of artifact-free EEG were analyzed with EEGLAB (MATLAB). To facilitate between-subject comparisons, EEG recordings were standardized using z-score normalization. The normalized EEG data were segmented into 5-s epochs for PSD estimation using the pwelch function from the MATLAB Signal Processing Toolbox, applying a 5-s Hamming window to minimize spectral leakage [13]. The final PSD was computed by averaging PSD values across all epochs. Relative power was calculated as the power at each frequency divided by the total power within the 0–55 Hz range. Data analysis was focusing on frequency bands from delta (0–3 Hz), theta (4–7 Hz), alpha (8–12 Hz), beta (13–25 Hz) to gamma (>40 Hz).

sec.title: Quantitative Sensory Testing
sec.p: Thermal Quantitative Sensory Testing (QST) was performed at baseline and within 1 month after FUS. QST was conducted on the forearm of the painful side using the Medoc TSA-II device (Medoc Ltd., Ramat Yishai, Israel). A method-of-limits protocol was used to assess detection thresholds for cold (CD) and warm (WD) stimuli, as well as pain thresholds for cold (CP) and heat (HP) stimuli [14]. All stimuli started at a baseline temperature of 32°C and changed at a 1°C/second ramp rate. Participants indicated when they detected a temperature change (CD, WD) or experienced pain (CP, HP). Cutoff temperatures were set at 0°C for CP and 50°C for HP. Each threshold was measured 5 times, with the highest and lowest values discarded; the final threshold was calculated as the average of the remaining three values. Raw threshold values were compared to age-matched reference data from the German Research Network on Neuropathic Pain database [15]. Thresholds exceeding two standard deviations from reference values were classified as abnormal, indicating potential dysfunction in A-delta and/or C afferent fibers and/or their central processing [14].

sec.title: Somatosensory Evoked Potentials
sec.p: At baseline and 1 month postsurgically, median nerve somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs) were recorded (stimulus: pulse width 0.2 milliseconds, 3.1 Hz, intensity visible thumb twitch; recording: 1,000 repetitions, 3 trials, sample rate 1,000 Hz, filter bandpass 30–500 Hz). Recording sites included Erb’s point, C6 spinous process, and scalp C3, C4, and FM in accordance with international SSEP recording guidelines. Key responses included N9/Erb’s point, N13/spinal root entry, and N20/P25 somatosensory cortex. Absolute and N20-EP interpeak latencies were obtained.

sec.title: Patient Characteristics
sec.p: Twelve adult patients were eligible for participation and signed consent. Seven declined participation or were screening failures (online suppl. data; for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/000547639) and 5 were treated (Table 1). All 5 were men (mean age = 64.2 ± 10.4 years) with pain related to head and neck cancer (mean duration of pain was 13.2 ± 10.4 months). The pains were predominantly unilateral or very asymmetric and often heterogenous with both nociceptive and neuropathic pain qualities. The location of pain was trigeminal, cervical, tonsillar, or oropharyngeal. The pain was unilateral neuropathic, nociceptive, or both except for 1 patient who had an asymmetric visceral pain in the throat after radiation therapy. Pain was refractory to oral medications, including opioids, but two of the patients were hospitalized for parenteral opioid analgesia and two others underwent percutaneous trigeminal rhizotomy without benefit.

fn.p: SCC, squamous cell carcinoma; V2, trigeminal maxillary division; V3, trigeminal mandibular division.
aInpatient: required hospitalization for parental analgesia (i.e., opioids, ketamine, lidocaine) prior to FUS.

sec.title: FUS Procedure
sec.p: Midbrain ablations were achieved for all 5 patients. In general, the procedures were well tolerated, and frame placement was performed with light sedation. Subject 006 had a tracheostomy and was heavily sedated for the procedure due to his pain and anxiety. Subject 009 became agitated toward the end of the procedure, receiving intravenous midazolam and dexmedetomidine. His agitation seemed to resolve after the procedure with a cigarette.

Final acoustic energies for ablation (range 13 k–30 k), final average target temperatures (range 52–59°C), and treatment times were similar to a FUS thalamotomy procedure for tremor (online suppl. Table S1). Between 1 and 3 ablations were made, either medial targeting the border of the periaqueductal gray for the spinoreticular tract or laterally targeting the spinothalamic tract (online suppl. Table S2). The stereotactic coordinates and volumes of the lesions were assessed on day 1 and are reported in online supplementary Table S3.

sec.title: Study Conduct
sec.p: All subjects succumbed to their cancer during the study, so post-procedural assessments were limited. Only subject 009 completed all assessments. Complete cancer-related morbidity, including serious adverse events and mortality, is listed in online supplementary Tables S4 and S5.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Procedural morbidity is reported in Table 2. The most common side effect was contralateral numbness presumably from the ablation or perilesional edema encroaching anteriorly to the medial lemniscus. This was observed in 3 patients; all reported that it was mild, nonbothersome, or transient. Subject 009 reported horizontal diplopia the day following the procedure that resolved within 3 weeks. There were 2 cases of altered level of consciousness. Subject 010 was obtunded for a day. Within 4 days, his somnolence had resolved and he was alert and at his baseline. Subject 009 became agitated during the procedure, somewhat resolving by smoking a cigarette after the procedure.

sec.title: Pain
sec.p: Pain scores are reported in Table 3. All subjects had a substantial reduction in pain intensity the day after the FUS procedure. According to our predetermined definition, three of the five were classified as responders with a 50% reduction in pain intensity at last follow-up.

fn.p: A summary of numerical pain rating scores (“0” no pain and “10” is the worst pain). Note that 3 of the 5 subjects (005, 006, 010) were considered “responders” to the FUS mesencephalotomy as their pain scores improved by over 50% at the last follow-up visit.

sec.p: Some anecdotal case observations are described for this small cohort. Subject 002 had an immediate relief of his facial grimace and was able to open his mouth immediately in the procedure after the therapeutic ablation, but this improvement lasted less than 48 h. Subject 005 had immediate pain relief with the procedure, and his wife reported at day 76 that “the one saving grace was that he passed away pain free from the effects of the FUS procedure. He was only taking tramadol a couple of timesper day, but really felt a world of difference.” Subject 010 was obtunded from the procedure. When he awakened the next day, he reported pain relief and was able to wean from intravenous hydromorphone (morphine equivalent dose from 600 mg to 9 mg) during 2 weeks in the hospital. His palliative care physician later reported at day 33: “He’s now on hospice. The family was raving about the focused ultrasound. He has very minimal pain and compared to the agony he was in, it is just amazing.”

sec.title: Other Outcomes
sec.p: Other patient-reported, PROMIS measures are reported in online supplementary Figure S1. Otherwise, there were no consistent findings except a trend toward improvement with physical function. Because of the small sample size and limited follow-up, a statistical analysis is not provided for the primary efficacy outcome nor other pain measures.

sec.title: Resting-State EEG
sec.p: Resting-state EEG analysis of adequate quality was obtained for 4 subjects (002, 005, 009, and 010). There were no consistent changes in delta, theta, alpha, or beta frequency band power distributions after FUS mesencephalotomy for either treatment responders or nonresponders. However, gamma band power showed a significant pattern of being increased in responders and decreased in nonresponders (p < 0.001) (Fig. 2).

caption.p: Resting-state EEG before and after FUS mesencephalotomy. Averaged power spectrum from resting-state EEG before and after FUS mesencephalotomy for treatment responders (above) and nonresponders (below). Power (dB) is on the Y-axis and frequency (Hz) is on the X-axis (up to 55 Hz). Statistical comparisons between pre- and post-treatment for the dominant, delta (0.5–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz), beta (13–30 Hz), and gamma (30–100 Hz) frequency bands are shown in inset plots (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.05). Significant differences are indicated by an asterisk (*).

sec.p: The frequency of the posterior dominant waking rhythm (PDR) significantly decreased in treatment FUS responders but not in nonresponders (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p < 0.05). For responders, the baseline PDR frequency had a median of 7.8 Hz (IQR: 6.9–8.6 Hz), while the post-treatment median was 7.3 Hz (IQR: 6.3–8.2 Hz). For nonresponders, the baseline PDR frequency had a median of 8.0 Hz (IQR: 7.1–8.9 Hz), and the post-treatment median was 8.0 Hz (IQR: 7.0–8.9 Hz).

sec.title: Thermal Quantitative Sensory Testing
sec.p: QST was performed for 4 subjects (S002, S005, S006, and S009). The baseline QST results from S002, S006, and S009 showed significant thermal sensation deficits, including elevated detection thresholds and reduced pain thresholds for both cold and heat stimuli. In contrast, no thermal sensation deficits were identified in subject 005.

Postsurgically, treatment nonresponders S002 and S009 showed improved QST results, with S002 exhibiting normalizations of WD and HP thresholds, and S009 achieving normal CP and HP thresholds, suggesting an incomplete spinothalamic tract lesion. In contrast, treatment responder S005, who had normal pre-treatment QST results, developed thermal pain and detection deficits across all test stimuli, while the other treatment responder, S006, developed an additional abnormal CP threshold (online suppl. Fig. S2). These findings suggest effective spinothalamic lesioning in responders.

sec.title: Somatosensory Evoked Potentials
sec.p: SSEPs before and after treatment were obtained from 3 subjects (S005, S006, and S010). Baseline SSEPs demonstrated normal absolute and interpeak latencies. Subject 006 developed contralateral numbness following FUS mesencephalotomy as the lesion extended anteriorly towards the medial lemniscus; his SSEP, accordingly, demonstrated loss of the cortical N20 potential (online suppl. Fig. S3). Subject 005 also developed contralateral numbness following the procedure, but the preservation of the cortical N20 potential indicated that ascending fibers from the posterior columns and medial lemniscus remained sufficiently intact to conduct ascending signals to the somatosensory cortex. Subject 010 did not develop a sensory deficit and his SSEP remained preserved (online suppl. Table S6).

sec.title: Radiofrequency Mesencephalotomy Case
sec.p: During the study, 1 subject was excluded because his skull density ratio of 0.28 was insufficient for transmitting acoustic energy. He was a 60-year-old with squamous cell carcinoma of the oropharynx invading into the inner ear. The cancer had been treated earlier in the year with radiation therapy, cisplatin, and pembrolizumab. He developed a prominent neuropathic pain that was described constant burning around the ear and lower face with a preservation of facial sensation. He was hospitalized and treated with parenteral hydromorphone, lidocaine, ketamine, and a percutaneous trigeminal radiofrequency rhizotomy. He eventually underwent a successful, frame-based, radiofrequency mesencephalotomy with two ablations of 70° and 80°C for 60 s each. Postoperatively, he was somnolent for 1 day and then aroused without pain and was able to wean substantially from pain medications to methadone only. His morphine equivalent dose decreased from 292 mg to 45 mg. This case is included as a comparison of midbrain, thermal lesioning modalities (Fig. 3).

caption.p: Stereotactic thermal ablations of the dorsal midbrain for cancer pain. Radiofrequency mesencephalotomy (left) allows for ablation along the axis of the dorsal midbrain, but there is risk of intracerebral injury from electrode insertion (white arrow). Adjustments for electrical stimulation mapping or ablation require additional brain penetration. FUS mesencephalotomy (right) does not involve penetration of the brain, but the shape of the ablation is dependent on the ultrasound transducer – leading to an elongated lesion in the anterior-posterior direction.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this early feasibility clinical trial designed for safety and tolerability, 5 patients with head and neck cancer pain were treated with stereotactic FUS mesencephalotomy. These patients had craniocervical pain above C5 and were obviously not candidates for other cancer pain procedures like spinal cordotomy or intrathecal infusions. First, transcranial high-intensity FUS energy was delivered to create midbrain lesions, and the procedure was tolerated by patients during advanced stages of cancer. Second, procedural morbidity occurred, but this fortunately resolved in most cases or was mild and non-bothersome. Importantly, 3 of the patients had substantial pain relief from the procedure for the remainder of their lives with over 50% reduction in their pain intensity scores when all other medical and interventional pain therapies had failed.

Stereotactic mesencephalotomy for the palliation of cancer pain is not new. Historical series before the era of MRI documented short-term pain relief for refractory cancer pain, but the procedure was limited by procedural morbidity [11]. More modern series of radiofrequency mesencephalotomy reported successful cases with less morbidity [16–22], but the small numbers of cases do not exclude the possibility of publication bias. Contemporary radiofrequency mesencephalotomy utilizing frame-based stereotaxy, semi-direct MRI-guided targeting, and intraoperative testing resulted in minimal complications and excellent/good pain relief at 12 months for 77% of 22 cancer pain patients [22].

The most common side effect in the present study of FUS mesencephalotomy was contralateral numbness, presumably from the treatment extending anteriorly toward the medial lemniscus [23]. One case in our series experienced numbness despite having intact cortical SSEPs; we speculate that this lesion spared enough ascending fibers to facilitate a cortical response. Extraocular dysmotility, almost expected with early series of radiofrequency mesencephalotomy [24], was substantially reduced by targeting the midbrain at the level below the superior colliculus [25]. Only 1 patient here had mild and transient horizontal diplopia. Perhaps the most unpredictable side effect in this series was temporary altered consciousness. One patient was obtunded for 24 h, returning to his normal level of arousal within a couple of days. Another patient became agitated during the treatment and then again in the evening while hospitalized. Definitive attribution of the cause of the agitation is not possible, as the participant was in active nicotine withdrawal, and the agitation generally resolved after he smoked a cigarette. However, it is notable that there was an ablation in the reticular activating region, which has a prominent role in regulating arousal and mood [26]. Alteration of consciousness has not been well described in larger series of RF mesencephalotomy [20, 21, 27, 28] although a persisting case of agitation and confusion was reported after a retreatment [22].

A comparison of radiofrequency and FUS lesioning notes key differences when targeting the mesencephalon. Both represent thermal ablations with immediate effects. Radiofrequency lesions can be localized first with electrical stimulation testing, but subsequent testing is problematic and often confounded with electrode repositioning. Radiofrequency testing and lesioning are constrained to the trajectory of the inserted electrode, and electrode insertion can be associated with cortical or intracerebral injury. Theoretically, FUS mapping and lesioning are easily adjusted with millimeter/submillimeter increments in any dimension, but testing uses less reliable, subthreshold heating, and therapeutic ablation is somewhat shape dependent by current transducer design. Our experience with low-intensity FUS neuromodulation for brain mapping has not been convincing.

Regardless of the surgical technique, the optimal pain target for midbrain lesioning remains to be determined. Conceptually, the dorsal midbrain is ideal with its confluence of ascending pain fibers and the descending pain regulation system. Nociceptive-responsive neurons have been identified here with single-cell microelectrode recordings [10]. The origins of mesencephalic lesioning for pain targeted the laterally positioned, spinothalamic tract [4] that could be somatotopically localized with electrical stimulation [9]. Mesencephalic spinothalamic tractotomy evolved from a posterior approach through the tectum [5, 9] to a frontal approach with less morbidity [6, 19, 28]. A more medial, “extralemniscal” lesion bordering the periaqueductal gray was proposed from extensive midbrain mapping including with chronically implanted electrodes [6, 7, 10]. Lesions of this medial region (termed both stereotactic mesencephalotomy or rostral mesencephalic reticulotomy) presumably include the spinoreticular pathway with relief of the suffering and emotional dimension of pain akin to a cingulotomy [6, 7, 10, 28, 29]. Marques et al. [22] varied their lesion laterality depending on the tract to be targeted and the location of the pain. In this trial of FUS mesencephalotomy, we initially lesioned the traditional “extralemniscal” target, but the benefit was temporary. There was substantial pain relief for 2 subsequent patients with lateral lesioning, presumably interrupting the spinothalamic tract. FUS mesencephalotomy allows for targeting both midbrain regions without the risks from multiple electrode insertions.

Neurophysiological assessments were obtained with the goal of quantifying cortical biomarkers of pain relief. Albeit limited by the small number of patients, responders exhibited an increase in EEG gamma power and nonresponders a decrease. The increase in gamma activity among responders aligns with studies that link gamma oscillations to sensory integration and cortical reorganization [30], suggesting that adaptive neuroplasticity may occur following lesioning of the spinothalamic tract. Conversely, the reduction in gamma power among nonresponders may indicate an alternative pattern of neural adaptation, potentially involving ineffective reorganization or altered thalamocortical processing. Additionally, the PDR decreased in responders but not in nonresponders. Our interpretation is that pain relief may be related to a loss-of-function change – i.e., an effective ascending tract lesion that can be measured cortically – that is beneficial in short term. This interpretation is supported by the loss of the cortical potential in SSEP in one of the responders. A longer observation period (e.g., >3 months) may be necessary to further investigate potential neurophysiological changes over time [31].

Treatment responders developed expected thermal sensation deficits by QST, indicating a successful lesion. While heat allodynia is commonly observed in chronic cancer pain populations, both treatment nonresponders in this study exhibited cold allodynia, which was absent in treatment responders. This finding may suggest a distinct pathophysiological subtype of chronic pain [32, 33] where cold allodynia indicates a pain phenotype that is less responsive to mesencephalotomy. Thermal sensory profiling may serve as a predictor of individual responsiveness to FUS mesencephalotomy with both thermal hypoesthesia and allodynia serving as key indicators for effective treatment.

This clinical trial has limitations. The sample size is small; and the study follow-up was abbreviated as patients failed to meet the final assessment visit. Patients who were referred for this early-stage clinical trial suffered with advanced cancer as evidenced by their disease-related morbidities and mortalities during the 3-month study duration. Nevertheless, FUS mesencephalotomy was tolerated during the late stages of cancer and near the end of life. A connectivity analysis with fMRI and diffusion tensor imaging was attempted with this unique lesioning process [34]; but the quality of the studies was limited by the cohort, the acquisition of images immediately following treatment, and the lack of stable postoperative images when perilesional edema has resolved.

Even with the limitations of this initial preliminary clinical trial, we remain optimistic for the future of FUS mesencephalotomy. Contouring the ablation with the shape of the heating can be immediately adjusted by tilting the ultrasound transducer and applying filtered masks. Device innovation will likely allow for more complex target contouring and volumetric ablations. Other technological advances could allow for patient-specific treatments as diffusion tensor imaging and tractography enable the visualization of spinothalamic, medial lemniscus, and possibly spinoreticular pathways in the brainstem [35, 36]; and the integrity or interruptions of these tracts could be determined with electrophysiological monitoring using somatosensory and laser-evoked potentials. Stereotactic FUS mesencephalotomy can be tolerated even in the later stages of cancer and for patients with respiratory insufficiency who may otherwise have risks with high cervical cordotomy ablations.

In conclusion, high-intensity FUS was used to ablate the dorsal midbrain, providing promising pain relief in a small cohort with advanced cancer pain. A future clinical trial is underway to better assess safety and efficacy of the procedure. More experience will help to refine the indications for the procedure and the optimal target for treatment.
